entry.title: 5 Common Clarity Development Mistakes (And How to Fix Them)
entry.summary: Forgetting the . Prefix When Calling Contracts The mistake: lisp In Clarity, every contract is identified by its deployer address and contract name. When you're working in the Clarinet console, the . before a contract name (e.g., .counter) is shorthand for the fully qualified identifier — it tells Clarity to look for the contract deployed by the current transaction sender. Without the . prefix, Clarity has no idea which contract you're referring to. The fix: lisp Using Wrong Integer Types (1 vs u1) The mistake: lisp Clarity has two distinct integer types: int The fix: lisp Missing Parentheses The mistake: lisp Clarity uses Lisp-style syntax, where every expression is wrapped in parentheses. Coming from languages like JavaScript or Python, this takes some getting used to. The fix: lisp Confusing let and define-data-var The mistake: Using define-data-var when you just need a temporary local variable, or expecting Why it happens: define-data-var creates persistent on-chain storage that lives as long as the contract exists lisp let for temporary calculations define-data-var for state that persists Not Handling none from Map Lookups The mistake: lisp map-get? returns an optional type — either The fix: lisp Wrapping Up Resources to keep learning: .
